topic: The Inscribed Square Problem: A Topological Journey
target_audience: Undergraduate students or advanced high school students with an interest in geometry

outline.topic: The Inscribed Square Problem: A Topological Journey
outline.target_audience: Undergraduate students or advanced high school students with an interest in geometry

sections.title: The Hook: The Pirate's Square Treasure
sections.content: Introduce the central question: For any simple, closed loop (Jordan curve), can we always find four points on that loop that form the vertices of a perfect square? This is known as the Toeplitz Conjecture.
sections.example: An explorer finds a wobbly, irregular island coastline. He wants to place four observation towers at the corners of a perfect square along the shore. No matter how jagged the coast is, can he always do it?

sections.title: Prerequisite: Defining the 'Jordan Curve'
sections.content: Explain what a Jordan curve is: a non-self-intersecting continuous loop in a plane. Use visual animations to show the difference between a simple loop (like a rubber band) and a complex one (like a figure-eight, which is not a Jordan curve).
sections.example: Visualizing a 'wobbly circle' that can be stretched and pulled like dough, but never torn or crossed over itself.

sections.title: The Stepping Stone: The Inscribed Rectangle
sections.content: Before tackling the square, we look at the rectangle. This is a proven theorem. We introduce the concept of 'Pairs of Points'. Any two points on the curve define a potential side or diagonal.
sections.example: An ant and a beetle crawl along the loop. We track their positions and the distance between them to find symmetry.

sections.title: The Topological Trick: The Möbius Strip Mapping
sections.content: Introduce the brilliant proof for rectangles. We map every pair of points $(A, B)$ on the curve to a point in 3D space. The set of all unordered pairs of points on a circle topologically forms a Möbius Strip. We show how the 'boundary' of the curve maps to the edge of the strip.
sections.example: An animation showing a flat loop being transformed into a 3D Möbius strip. When this strip is dipped into a plane, the intersections represent the vertices of our rectangle.

sections.title: The Core Logic: Why One Surface Must Intersect Another
sections.content: Explain that because a Möbius strip has a boundary that maps to the curve itself, any surface spanning that boundary must intersect itself or a specific plane. This intersection point in the abstract 'space of pairs' corresponds to a set of points that form a rectangle in the real world.
sections.example: Imagine trying to flatten a crumpled piece of paper (the Möbius strip) onto a table. Because of its twist, it is forced to overlap itself; those overlaps are the secret locations of our rectangle corners.

sections.title: The Final Mystery: Square vs. Rectangle
sections.content: Discuss the current status of the problem. While rectangles are guaranteed for all Jordan curves, the 'Square' version is proven for smooth curves (like those drawn with a pen) but remains one of topology's famous unsolved problems for 'fractal' or extremely jagged curves.
sections.example: A comparison between a smooth 'potato' shape (where a square is easily found) and a snowflake-like fractal coastline where mathematicians are still searching for the definitive proof.

sections.title: Conclusion: The Power of Topology
sections.content: Summarize how looking at a problem from a higher dimension (moving from 2D curves to 3D surfaces like the Möbius strip) can solve puzzles that seem impossible in the original space.
sections.example: The explorer from Section 1 realizes that by looking at the 'map' of all possible pairs, the solution to his tower placement was hidden in the geometry of the paper itself.

storyboard.title: The Hook: The Pirate's Square Treasure
lecture_lines: Can every closed loop contain four vertices of a square?
This mystery is known as the Toeplitz Conjecture.
Imagine placing four towers on a jagged island's coast.
animations: A light blue (#ADD8E6) irregular Jordan curve fades in centrally.
Four yellow (#FFFF00) dots appear at random positions on the curve.
The dots connect to form a yellow quadrilateral with thin lines.
The dots slide along the curve until they form a perfect green (#00FF00) square.
The text 'Toeplitz Conjecture' appears in white (#FFFFFF) below the curve.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: Defining the 'Jordan Curve'
lecture_lines: A Jordan curve is a simple, non-self-intersecting loop.
It can be wobbly like a rubber band.
However, it can never cross over itself like this.
animations: A simple white (#FFFFFF) circle appears; label 'Jordan Curve' fades in.
The circle smoothly deforms into a wobbly shape without self-intersecting.
A red (#FF0000) figure-eight appears with a red 'X' to show it is NOT a Jordan curve.

storyboard.title: The Stepping Stone: The Inscribed Rectangle
lecture_lines: Let's first look for rectangles instead of squares.
Any two points on the loop define a possible side.
We track the midpoint and distance between these points.
animations: An irregular light blue (#ADD8E6) loop is shown with two orange (#FFA500) dots A and B.
Two more orange dots C and D appear, forming a rectangle ABCD on the curve.
The rectangle rotates and scales while all four vertices stay on the loop.

storyboard.title: The Topological Trick: The Möbius Strip Mapping
lecture_lines: We map pairs of points into a 3D space.
Unordered pairs on a circle form a Möbius strip.
The curve's points map to the strip's boundary edge.
This topological transformation reveals hidden geometric connections.
Watch how the loop twists into a 3D surface.
animations: A gray (#808080) square represents the space of all point pairs (A, B).
The diagonal (A=B) is highlighted in white (#FFFFFF) as the curve itself.
Arrows appear on the square's edges showing identification with a twist.
The square morphs into a 2D representation of a Möbius strip (#DA70D6).
The boundary of the Möbius strip is highlighted in bright white (#FFFFFF).

storyboard.title: The Core Logic: Why One Surface Must Intersect Another
lecture_lines: Every surface spanning this boundary must intersect itself.
These intersection points represent two pairs sharing properties.
If the properties match, we've found our rectangle.
The twist in the Möbius strip forces this overlap.
Topology guarantees these specific points must exist.
animations: The orchid (#DA70D6) Möbius strip is shown overlapping a horizontal plane.
Bright white (#FFFFFF) intersection points appear where the strip meets the plane.
An intersection point is highlighted, mapping back to four points on the curve.
These four points on the original loop connect to form an orange (#FFA500) rectangle.
The rectangle flashes green (#00FF00) to signify a valid solution.

storyboard.title: The Final Mystery: Square vs. Rectangle
lecture_lines: Rectangles always exist, but what about perfect squares?
For smooth curves, the answer is a proven "yes".
But for fractal-like jagged curves, the mystery remains.
Mathematicians are still searching for a definitive proof.
Is there always a square on every possible loop?
animations: A smooth green (#00FF00) curve is shown with a clear inscribed square.
A jagged, red-orange (#FF4500) fractal curve replaces the smooth one.
A large yellow (#FFFF00) question mark fades in over the fractal curve.

storyboard.title: Conclusion: The Power of Topology
lecture_lines: Topology lets us solve 2D puzzles using higher dimensions.
Higher surfaces reveal answers hidden in simple planes.
Some geometric secrets are still waiting to be discovered.
animations: The original loop and its green (#00FF00) square from section 1 return.
The Möbius strip representation pulses slowly in the background.
Final text 'The Power of Topology' fades in centrally in white (#FFFFFF).
